I admit that I didn't test it too extensively, but I'd expect it to work (to the degree that Windows allows it using non-unicode APIs). I may do more testing, but here is some more background:

- on mingw build
When you do std::ofstream(str, ...), standard c++ library will end up calling one of msvcrt.*open variants, passing your string argument. Windows internally uses utf-16 for things like file names, so it needs to be converted to utf-16 at some point. In this case, msvcrt will then convert the string to urf-16 using default system codepage (CP_ACP) and pass that to lower level functions (CreateFileW). So if A->utf16 uses CP_ACP, utf16->A should also use CP_ACP for things to work reliably.

Obviously, current codepage may or may not support CJK. But if it doesn't, there is no way we may support that using ansi-based APIs. This is general limitation of the way those APIs work on Windows (and Wine needs to be compatible with Windows in this aspect). Passing utf8 string will not help in this case, because Windows will interpret that as different codepage anyway (well, unless utf8 is the system codepage).

The only way to avoid the problem is to avoid all conversions. It would require using utf16 APIs like kernel32 CreateFileW or msvcrt _wopen. There is no portable C++ way of doing that. MSVC C++ library allows passing wchar_t strings to constructors and functions, but GCC stdc++ does not. There are some tricks like what Mozilla does:
https://hg.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/file/tip/mfbt/FStream.h#l32
but I don't think that's worth it in case of dxvk.

- on winelib build
std::ofstream just ends up calling glibc's open. There are no Windows paths nor Windows encoding involved. It's just plain UNIX path name. Linux treats file names just as byte strings and does not attempt to do any conversions or decoding. It's standard practice that those byte strings are interpreted using configured encoding and that's what Wine's CP_UNIXCP extension uses. Those days it probably means utf8 for majority users, but it depends on configuration.

Do we have any sort of guarantee that setting the registry key can never go wrong and that we'll never have stale entries in the registry even when something crashed during a previous launch? If not, we really shouldn't be creating an infinite loop here.

> Why does the current code not work outside of some potential race conditions if the app initializes both at the same time? We shouldn't touch initialization unless `getGenericInterface` fails to return a compositor.

Yes, you are right, assuming DXVK gets the same higher level openvr_api.dll loader as the game is using (which stores the global vrclient's interface pointer during initialization and will succeed the interface query if the initialization has already been performed through VR_InitInternal[2] from this dll). That must be usually the case in practice, the other cases are more of theoretical concern and I probably shouldn't have mentioned this part.

The real issue which I currently saw affecting games is the extra initialization and teardown of vrclient done in the game process.

> 
> I'm not really a big fan of this solution either since it heavily depends on external factors working correctly, which also seems more than a little bit fragile.

Yes, doing the same VR client init / tear down outside of game requests is still not ideal (as vrclient links some things to steam game id also), but looks less fragile than doing the same in the game process.

> Do we have any sort of guarantee that setting the registry key can never go wrong and that we'll never have stale entries in the registry even when something crashed during a previous launch? If not, we really shouldn't be creating an infinite loop here.

The guarantee from any leftovers from the previous launch is using the volatile keys, they are not stored anywhere persistently and do not exist after Proton prefix shutdown, so upon new start the HKCU\\Software\\Wine\\VR key never exists until created by Proton's steam.exe. Unless someone sets it manually of course, but I believe we already have enough ways of breaking things manually like that anyway.

The more concerning part is probably the extension query process with VR init in initialize_vr_data() in steam.exe (in the attached patch). But I believe it is effectively equivalent to what DXVK currently does, so if something is going to hang there and leave status '0' the same seems to have equal chances to happen on the same route DXVK. If SteamVR is not running or libraries are not available we should be setting the ~0u status quickly, and it is rather hard to guess what can go wrong on this path unless some fundamental things (like setting registry key) are not working in Proton prefix.

I thought of adding some sort of timeout, but that timeout must be rather big. FWIW, with the way currently in DXVK the initialization takes ~2 sec in many cases when SteamVR is running with Steam's vrclient log complaining about timeout waiting for valid appkey after 2 sec. I am avoiding that now in steam.exe VR init, but not entirely sure such thing cannot happen under some different conditions. I decided to check just to make sure that this assurance holds; here's my sketch of a proof for it:

Given:
1. The D3D11Query implementation uses a simple, lock-protected FSM to guarantee that it alternates between starting Begin and End operations: an out-of-order Begin is discarded, and an out-of-order End has a Begin injected before it.
2. Operations are sent to the CS thread and dispatched in strict FIFO order (I am not 100% on this)
3. D3D11Query also has an atomic counter that accurately tracks the number of in-flight End operations.

Therefore:
- The D3D `GetData()` implementation will only attempt to call the underlying query's `getData()` if it is in the "ended" state (meaning the most recent operation started was an End, per given 1) and there are no in-flight End operations (per given 3). And, if the most recently started operation is no longer in-flight, then no other operations are in-flight (per given 2) at all. Also, the atomic-sub has release semantics, and the `GetData()`'s implied atomic-load defaults to seq_cst, so data is also properly synchronized.

Unless I am missing something, this means that there was no race between `DxvkGpuQuery::begin()`/`DxvkGpuQuery::end()` and `DxvkGpuQuery::getData()` in the first place! So making `m_ended` atomic may be redundant: perhaps you decide that's a good thing for robustness, but if not it's an unnecessary performance cost.

In general I prefer an all-or-nothing approach to making objects guarantee thread safety: `DxvkGpuQuery` should be responsible for all of its synchronization guarantees or none of them. That is, if we're going to require that callers guarantee that no `begin()` call is pending when calling `getData()`, we may as well also require that callers guarantee that no `end()` call is pending either. (And we are changing the `getData()` contract anyway by making it non-const, so it might be good to codify these requirements at the same time.)

If the ABI of SDL or GLFW changes incompatibly, then you already need to know about that and react to it, because the symbols that you list in [wsi_platform_sdl2_funcs.h](https://github.com/doitsujin/dxvk/pull/3834/files#diff-4ccb978d31117e5c2b73e6f2f3766f412b897cec609c1ad010950e38481cb0fe) and [wsi_platform_glfw_funcs.h](https://github.com/doitsujin/dxvk/pull/3834/files#diff-e109f7a3c9d6cbe0419f2dc9fce561cc2cf2cc81b814827bab5748ae73cee968) will need reviewing anyway. That's because one possible reason for an ABI break would be an incompatible change to the signature of one of those functions, for example if `GLFWmonitor **glfwGetMonitors(int *)` changed to `GLFWmonitor **glfwGetMonitors(size_t *)` in a newer version of GLFW.

The traditional build-system-developer answer, e.g. in `libtool`, would be "no you can't learn the SONAME, and it's wrong to want to", because shared libraries and `dlopen()`'able modules happen to be the same thing on popular platforms like Windows and Linux but have historically been implemented differently in some OSs. In that view of the world, each shared object is either correct to link like `-lSDL3` or correct to dlopen like `dlopen("/path/to/myplugin.so")`, but never both; and the pedantically correct approach would be for DXVK to have in-tree plugins for SDL and GLFW (no need for a stable API/ABI between library and plugin), similar to how libdecor has in-tree plugins for Cairo and GTK. In that design, the plugin would be the only thing that is dlopened, and the plugin would have a normal DT_NEEDED dependency (hard dependency) on the library it uses.

But, assuming that you have no interest in making DXVK run on AIX or HPUX or whatever other museum piece has this limitation, I can see why you would prefer to cut out the middle-man and dlopen the library itself!

It looks as though SDL's `FindLibraryAndSONAME` assumes that if you take the `basename` of the `realpath` of the shared library, and then truncate `libfoo.so.1.2.3.4` to `libfoo.so.1`, the result is the SONAME. This is not strictly correct - some libraries, confusingly, have SONAME `libfoo.so.0` and a symlink `libfoo.so.0 -> libfoo.so.1.2.3.4` - but it "often" works correctly for "normal" libraries.

It **only** ignores the offset when calling `IDirect3DStateBlock9::Capture`.
That means, that both the initial capture when creating a state block using `IDirect3DDevice9::CreateStateBlock` as well as capturing the stream source by calling `IDirect3DDevice9::SetStreamSource` in between `IDirect3DDevice9::BeginStateBlock` and `IDirect3DDevice9::EndStateBlock` will capture the offset as one would normally expect.

`IDirect3DStateBlock9::Apply` only touches the stream sources if the state block has been created using `IDirect3DDevice9::CreateStateBlock(D3DSBT_VERTEXSTATE)` or by calling `IDirect3DDevice9::SetStreamSource` in between `IDirect3DDevice9::BeginStateBlock` and `IDirect3DDevice9::EndStateBlock`. So the only thing that does not work is **updating** the offset of a stream source that is capturing in a state block by calling `Capture`. The PS Mask is only considered late if we find hazards that otherwise can't be resolved by unbinding the render target. 

The goal of that is to avoid breaking up the render pass on shader changes.
Dead Space 2 runs into this (with depth stencil but it's the same general idea):
- Draw with shader that samples texture => DS gets bound as readonly
- Draw with shader that does not sample texture => DS gets bound as RW
- Repeat

Same thing with RTs would be:
- Write mask for RT1 is 0
- Draw with shader that samples RT1 texture => RT1 gets unbound
- Draw with shader that does not sample RT1 texture => RT1 gets bound
- Repeat

Ignoring the `psMasks.samplerMask` means we'd still have a resolvable hazard there with the second shader, so it would keep RT1 unbound instead of binding it again and thus get rid of all those barriers.

D3DKMT handles may be local or global. The local handles are process private and represent either a non-shared D3DKMT object or a shared global object opened in a process. Each local handle owns a reference to the global object in the latter case.

Global D3DKMT handles are shareable directly across process and they are the "old" way of sharing D3DKMT objects (the "KMT" Vulkan handle types).

The "new" way of sharing D3DKMT (D3D11_1+) is through NT shared handles (the non-KMT Vulkan handle types), which also own a reference to the global D3DKMT object. The NT shared handles are private to a process but can be duplicated or closed using the standard Windows DuplicateHandle / CloseHandle APIs.

These NT shared handles are allocated by calling D3DKMTShareObjects (which allows to provide a name, possibly different one on each call and share the same object multiple times under a different name), and that function takes D3DKMT local handles.
